stages.name: test controller
stages.what: pytest orchestrates: picks the DUT port, launches the process, sequences tests, collects results.
stages.why: On a real rig this is the test executive — the thing that owns the run and the bench.
stages.failures: Two controllers on one bench corrupt each other's run — hence exclusive resource ownership.

stages.name: stimulus
stages.what: LabClient drives inputs: status requests, malformed bytes, timing pressure, concurrent load.
stages.why: Stimulus must be deterministic and logged, or a failure cannot be reproduced.
stages.failures: Uncontrolled timing in stimulus (sleep-based waits) makes results environment-dependent.

stages.name: DUT
stages.what: The device under test — here the simulator; on a bench, real hardware with real I/O latency.
stages.why: The simulator shares your clock and OS; hardware does not. That gap is the whole reason HWIL exists.
stages.failures: Assumptions the simulator never violates (instant responses, perfect framing) fail first on hardware.

stages.name: telemetry
stages.what: Responses plus the DUT's own log: dut_ready, request/response lines, shutdown events, fault_injected lines.
stages.why: Telemetry is the DUT's side of the story — required to classify product vs harness failures.
stages.failures: Without DUT-side logs, a red test is one person's word against another's.

stages.name: capture / evaluation
stages.what: Assertions evaluate behavior; JUnit + logs + manifest capture the run for later audit.
stages.why: A lab result you cannot re-run or re-inspect is an anecdote, not evidence.
stages.failures: Evaluation without capture forces re-runs; capture without configuration identity makes re-runs meaningless.
